mappings.note: Outcome of Nepal's April 2006 movement. This item, and the 54 that follow, is from POPULAR STRUGGLES AND MOVEMENTS, misfiled into Political Parties; none of the 7 LOs here (party definition, ideology, party systems, national/State recognition, party reform) touches popular struggles, so the analysis competency C-3.3 is the honest level.
Identifies a pressure group. Institutional recall of a body that is explicitly NOT a party, so no party LO applies; C-3.1 rather than C-3.2-LO-1.
Example of a public interest group: recall of the sectional/public typology, which has no LO in this frame.
Composition of FEDECOR: recall of a case organisation, not analysis (C-3.3).
Which claim about public interest groups is false: tests the definition of the category, so recall-level C-3.1.
Who decisively makes a country's laws: the ruling party's legislators. This is a function of political parties, so LO-1 genuinely fits even though the item sits in the misfiled block.
Which statement about Nepal is untrue: recall of the case's facts, below C-3.3's analytic level.
The distinction between pressure groups and parties turns on what parties uniquely do: contest elections and seek power. That is LO-1's role-and-function territory, not LO-2's reform agenda.
Properties of sectional interest groups: category recall, no covering LO.
Cochabamba and water privatisation: recall of the case, not an evaluation of its outcome.
Asks what is true of the 2006 Nepal upsurge as a democratic event, so the analysis-of-democratic-practice competency rather than bare recall.
Names FEDECOR from its description: organisation recall, same level as qid:105541.
Names King Gyanendra: factual recall from the Nepal case.
What is true of public interest groups: category recall, as with qid:105542.
The form of government Nepal adopted in 1990: chronological/institutional recall.
Classifies FEDECOR as a public interest group: typology recall.
The aim of a public interest group (a collective rather than sectional good): definitional, so C-3.1.
Names the Bolivian party that took power in 2006. Not C-3.1-LO-7, which is confined to the Election Commission's Indian national/State criteria.
Asks what the Nepal and Bolivia struggles had in common: a comparison, hence the analysis competency, not the recall of either case separately.
Identifies the sectional interest group from its defining feature: category recall.
Which claim about pressure groups is untrue: definitional discrimination, C-3.1. Not C-3.2-LO-1, since no party function is in question.
The result of Bolivia's water war (contract cancelled, supply restored to the municipality) is the outcome of a democratic struggle, which is what C-3.3 covers.
Date Nepal first won democracy (1990): chronological recall.
How outstanding democratic conflicts get resolved (mass mobilisation): a general claim about democratic practice, C-3.3.
Names the World Bank as the agency that pressed for handing over municipal water supply: case recall.
Date King Gyanendra dismissed the prime minister and dissolved Parliament: chronological recall.
Year of the Nepalese royal massacre: chronological recall.
What the Bolivian people struggled against (water privatisation): recall of the case's object, not of its outcome (contrast qid:105559).
Which body is NOT an agency of organised politics: recall of the set of such agencies (parties, pressure groups, movements). No LO covers the set as a whole.
That democracy usually evolves through popular struggle is a claim about democratic practice, so C-3.3 rather than recall.
What the Kittiko-Hachchiko movement of 1987 was about: case recall from the movements section.
Who won Bolivia's water war: the struggle's outcome, C-3.3, as with qid:105559.

Names the Nepalese Maoists as the party that rejected parliamentary democracy yet joined the protest. Factual recall; C-3.1-LO-4 would require the candidate to reason from ideology to position rather than name the party.
What a 'defining moment' of democracy is a conflict between: an analytic claim about democratic practice, C-3.3.
Identifies a movement from a list: typology recall.
Names the Bolivian party that came to power in 2006: duplicate target of qid:105555.
Which organisation stayed out of the protest: case recall.
Which is NOT a sectional interest group: typology recall.
Which is NOT a movement: typology recall, the negative of qid:105573.
What sectional interest groups promote (the well-being of their own section): definitional.
Untrue claim about public interest groups: definitional discrimination, as with qid:105542.
Which is not a generic movement: recall of the generic/issue-specific movement distinction.
Untrue claim about Bolivia's Water War: recall of the case's facts, not an evaluation of its result.
Correct claim about sectional interest groups: category recall.
Asks for the MAIN reason behind the Water War among competing candidates, which requires weighing causes: analysis, C-3.3, unlike the plain recall of qid:105565.
The aim of Nepal's April 2006 movement (restoring democracy and a constituent assembly): the purpose of a democratic struggle, C-3.3.
Third duplicate of the 2006 Bolivian party item; factual recall.
Characterises the Bolivian people's struggle (a successful democratic mobilisation against privatisation), which is a judgement about democratic practice.
Date of Nepal's extraordinary popular movement: chronological recall.
How pressure groups and movements have DEEPENED democracy: an evaluation of democratic practice, C-3.3, and the clearest case in this block for the competency.
The relationship between parties and interest groups is part of the role parties play in organised politics, LO-1. Not LO-2, which is about reforming the party system.
Positive form of qid:105567; recall of the agencies of organised politics.
Fourth duplicate of the 2006 Bolivian party item; factual recall.
Names the Seven Party Alliance as the body that led Nepal's upsurge: case recall, not party-system theory.
Which parties have national-level organisation is the national/State distinction LO-7 draws. Not LO-5, which is about how many parties compete, not how they are recognised.
BSP's year and founder. Cited to LO-7 because BSP is one of the recognised national parties LO-7 asks the candidate to name; the item is the example half of that LO rather than its criteria half.
Asks the better route to political reform, which is LO-2 verbatim. Not LO-1, which describes what parties do rather than how the system should be changed.
BSP's inspiration from Sahu Maharaj, Phule, Periyar and Ambedkar is its ideology, and LO-4 is the LO about ideology shaping a party's positions. Not LO-7, which concerns recognition status.
Coalition government is the characteristic consequence of a multi-party system, which LO-5 distinguishes from one- and two-party systems. Not LO-6, which asks specifically why INDIA has many parties.
Which is NOT a component of a party tests the leaders / active members / followers triad that LO-3 names explicitly.
The recognition condition for a national party is the Election Commission criterion LO-7 names. Not LO-5: nothing about the number of competing parties is at issue.
Identifies a multi-party country, which is LO-5's 'gives an example of a country with each'.
When an alliance is formed: the mechanics of a multi-party system, LO-5. Not LO-6, which explains India's social basis for many parties.
BJP's guiding philosophy (cultural nationalism) is ideology, LO-4, not recognition status (LO-7).
Which party is NOT national: the national/State classification, LO-7.
Names BSP's founder; same national-party example target as qid:105594, so the same LO.
Identifies the one-party country (China), which is LO-5's example requirement for the single-party type.
Names the country democratic since independence (India). General recall; LO-6 would require the candidate to explain WHY India's social structure produces many parties, which this item does not ask.
The party espousing secularism and the welfare of weaker sections and minorities is identified from its ideological position, LO-4. Not LO-7, which turns on recognition criteria.
Which of these is NOT a political party tests the definition of a party, LO-3's first clause. Not LO-7, which sorts parties that already qualify.
The cause BSP stands for (the bahujan: Dalits, Adivasis, OBCs and minorities) is its ideological position, LO-4.
Naming the NDA as the 1998 alliance is the multi-party-system consequence LO-5 covers, as with qid:105601. Not LO-7: an alliance is not an Election Commission category.
NCP's stronghold state: a State party's regional base, which is the other half of LO-7's national/State distinction.
What is true of a country's party system in general: the one/two/multi-party typology, LO-5.
Classifying the Indian National Congress puts it in LO-7's national-party category. Not LO-4: no ideological position is asked for.
Which arrangement is not a good option for a democratic state: the one-party system, so the typology of LO-5. Not LO-2, since no reform is proposed.
BJP's founding year: recall about one of the recognised national parties LO-7 names.
The count of recognised national parties in 2006 follows directly from the Election Commission criteria of LO-7.
Identifies a two-party country, LO-5's example requirement for that type.
The 2004 alliances (NDA, UPA, Left Front) are the coalition politics of a multi-party system, LO-5.
Duplicate of qid:105605; identifies the one-party country, LO-5.
Parties granted an election symbol and other facilities are 'recognised' parties, which is precisely the Election Commission machinery LO-7 describes.

Which claim about CPI(M) is incorrect. Cited to LO-4 because the party is characterised in the chapter by its Marxism-Leninism and consequent positions; the options are not printed by the context tool, so the ideological limb is the best-supported reading.
Candidate selection is a named function of political parties, LO-1. Not LO-2, which is about reforming that function.
Parties putting forward policies and programmes for voters to choose from is the core function LO-1 describes.
CPI(M)'s states of strength: a party's regional base, the State-party side of LO-7, as with qid:105611.

Democracy's superiority in promoting dignity and freedom. This item and the 16 that follow are OUTCOMES OF DEMOCRACY content misfiled into Political Parties; the party LOs cannot be cited, and C-3.3 ('analyses and evaluates democratic practice and its OUTCOMES') is the exact competency for them.
Names the country held up as the model of accommodating social diversity. Factual recall of the example, so C-3.1 rather than the evaluative C-3.3 used for the surrounding items.
Which values carry moral and legal sanction in a democracy: an evaluation of what democracy delivers, C-3.3.
Why democracy's slowness in deciding is nevertheless worthwhile: a judgement weighing cost against benefit, C-3.3.
Which regime's decisions are more acceptable and effective: a comparative evaluation of outcomes, C-3.3.
What non-democratic government lacks (transparency and accountability): evaluation by contrast, C-3.3.
Which regime develops procedures to manage social competition: an outcome claim about democracy, C-3.3.
What democracies have successfully achieved: an evaluation of democratic outcomes, C-3.3.
Which regime best accommodates social diversity: comparative evaluation. Contrast qid:105628, which only asks for the example country.
Names the country where half the population is poor: statistical recall, not an evaluation of democracy's economic record (contrast qid:105639).
How economic benefits are distributed in democracies: the economic-outcomes limb of C-3.3.
Comparing growth rates under democratic and non-democratic regimes: evaluation of economic outcomes, C-3.3.
Why democracy is a better form of government: the central evaluative claim, C-3.3.
Why democratic decision-making is slow: analysis of a democratic outcome, C-3.3, the counterpart of qid:105630.
What studies show about political and social inequality under democracy: evaluation of outcomes against evidence, C-3.3.
